opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the most important questions right now. For a long time we could make progress by scraping the web, and the internet has a lot of general knowledge. But once you get into specialized domains like medicine, law, or finance, the really valuable knowledge isn't sitting on the open web. It lives in the heads of practitioners. It's in how a doctor reasons through an ambiguous case, what they rule out first, and what they notice that a textbook wouldn't tell you.

So the first step is that you need real experts in the loop. Early on, a lot of data annotation was done by generalists, and that was fine when you were teaching a model to be polite or follow basic instructions. Now we're asking models to operate at the level of a specialist, so you need specialists generating and evaluating the data. That's expensive. A physician's time is extremely valuable, so you can't just have thousands of doctors writing examples from scratch forever. It doesn't scale.

The way you scale it is by changing what you ask the expert to do. Instead of having them author everything, you have the model generate candidate answers or reasoning traces, and the expert critiques, corrects, and ranks them. Verifying is much faster than producing. A doctor can look at a model's differential diagnosis and say "you missed this," or "this is the wrong order of tests," in a fraction of the time it would take to write it out. That turns each hour of expert time into much more signal.

Then synthetic data multiplies it further. Once you have a strong seed set of expert-validated examples, and ideally some expert-written rubrics or principles for what good looks like, you can use models to generate many more variations around that core. They're grounded in the expert signal but expanded far beyond what humans could write by hand. The key is keeping humans as the anchor for quality, so you're not just amplifying the model's own mistakes.

The last piece is capturing expertise in deployment. When these systems are used in real workflows, with clinicians reviewing outputs and overriding the model when it's wrong, that feedback is incredibly rich. It's expertise exhibited in context, on real problems. If you can capture it responsibly, with privacy and consent handled properly, which matters enormously in medicine, you get a flywheel. The model gets better because experts use it, and experts use it more because it gets better.

So it's really a combination: expert-in-the-loop verification instead of pure authorship, synthetic expansion anchored to expert judgment, and feedback loops from real-world use. That's how you take something scarce, like a top specialist's judgment, and spread it across millions of interactions.

r001.rationale: The response says specialist time is expensive and that having thousands of doctors write examples from scratch does not scale.

r002.rationale: It describes models generating candidate answers and synthetic domain examples, but does not explain that training models to converse enables this generation.

r003.rationale: It proposes using expert-validated seed examples as a basis for generating many more synthetic variations.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss checking outputs in verifiable domains such as code or math to filter synthetic training data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot. The honest answer is that the bottleneck in a lot of specialized domains isn't compute or architecture anymore, it's the data. And in medicine specifically, the data you actually want, which is the reasoning of a really good clinician, isn't sitting on the internet. What's on the internet is textbooks and papers and forums, and that's useful, but it's not the same thing as watching how an experienced doctor works through an ambiguous case.

So the question becomes, how do you get that out of people's heads and into a form a model can learn from? And I think there are a few things that work.

The first is just being very deliberate about who you bring in. Early on, a lot of the industry treated annotation as a commodity. You'd hire a large pool of generalists and have them label things. That falls apart completely in medicine. You need people who are actually practitioners, and ideally practitioners across subspecialties, because a cardiologist and a dermatologist will look at the same patient summary and care about completely different things. We've invested pretty heavily in building out networks of domain experts, and I'd say that's one of the most underrated parts of the whole process.

The second piece is that the task you give these experts matters enormously. If you just ask them to write answers from scratch, you get very little per hour of expert time, and it's expensive time. What works much better is having the model generate first and having the expert critique, correct, and rank. That's a far more efficient use of someone's expertise, because evaluation is faster than generation, and it also captures something more subtle, which is the expert's judgment about what good looks like rather than just one example of a good answer. You're learning their preferences, not just their outputs.

Third, and this is where it gets interesting, you can use the model itself to amplify a small amount of expert signal. Once you have a few thousand high-quality expert-reviewed examples, you can train a model to approximate that judgment and use it to filter or score much larger pools of synthetic data. You have to be careful here, because synthetic data can drift and you can end up in a feedback loop where the model is reinforcing its own mistakes. So you keep the humans in the loop as a check, sampling and auditing continuously rather than annotating once and walking away.

And then the last thing I'd say is that for enterprise and healthcare deployments, a lot of the real expertise lives inside organizations, in their protocols, their case histories, their internal guidelines. So part of scaling expertise isn't about training data in the pretraining sense at all. It's about retrieval, giving the model access to that institutional knowledge at inference time, with citations, so a clinician can actually verify where an answer came from. In a domain like medicine, that verifiability matters as much as raw accuracy, because nobody is going to adopt a system they can't audit.

So I'd summarize it as: get real experts, use their time for judgment rather than generation, let the model amplify that signal carefully, and then ground the whole thing in the organization's own knowledge so the outputs are traceable. That combination is how you go from a model that sounds medical to one that's actually useful in a clinical setting.

r001.rationale: The response calls expert time expensive, but does not identify recruiting experts at scale as a barrier to training directly from their demonstrations.

r002.rationale: It describes models generating answers and synthetic data, but does not explain that training models to converse enables that generation.

r003.rationale: It says a small set of expert-reviewed examples can train a model to filter or score larger synthetic data pools, but does not propose expanding expert demonstrations into a larger synthetic training dataset.

r004.rationale: It discusses filtering synthetic data using learned expert judgment, but does not explain that correctness checks in verifiable domains such as code or math enable the filtering.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to use human expertise where it has the most impact. You don’t want a physician spending all their time labeling straightforward examples. You want them helping define what a good answer looks like, identifying subtle mistakes, and working through the cases where the model struggles.

Then you can build a feedback loop around that. A model can propose answers or generate variations on a case, and experts can critique them. Those critiques can become training signals that you apply across many more examples. So you’re trying to get more learning out of each hour of expert attention.

But in medicine, generating more data isn’t enough. You need to check that it’s accurate and that the model can handle genuinely new cases, rather than just reproduce patterns in its training data. I’d separate the process of creating training examples from the clinical evaluation of whether the resulting system is actually useful and safe.

r001.rationale: It says physicians should focus on high-impact work, but does not identify the cost of recruiting experts at scale as a barrier.

r002.rationale: It describes models proposing answers and generating case variations, but does not explain that training models to converse enables this synthetic data generation.

r003.rationale: It says expert critiques can provide training signals across more examples, but does not clearly propose expanding a small pool of trusted demonstrations into a much larger synthetic dataset.

r004.rationale: It calls for checking accuracy and evaluating clinical usefulness and safety, but does not describe using verifiable domains such as code or math to filter synthetic training data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to use experts where their judgment is most valuable. Having doctors write millions of examples from scratch is going to be expensive, and it takes time away from treating patients.

Instead, you can have a model propose an answer or work through a case, and ask an expert to critique it: What did it miss? Which assumption was wrong? What additional information should it have asked for? That gives you a much richer training signal than just labeling an answer right or wrong.

Then you can focus that process on cases where the model is uncertain or where models disagree. You’re using expert time to identify gaps, and using the model to help expand those lessons into more training examples. But in medicine, you have to validate that expansion carefully. Generating more data doesn’t necessarily mean you’re generating more knowledge; you could just be reproducing the same mistake.

So I’d think of it as a feedback loop: expert judgment, model training, rigorous evaluation, and then back to the experts on the failures that matter most.

r001.rationale: The response says having doctors write millions of examples from scratch is expensive and takes time away from treating patients.

r002.rationale: It describes models proposing answers for expert critique, but does not explain that training models to converse enables synthetic data generation.

r003.rationale: It says models can help expand lessons into more training examples, but does not specify expanding a small pool of trusted expert demonstrations into a much larger synthetic dataset.

r004.rationale: It calls for careful validation but does not mention verifiable domains such as code or math, or filtering synthetic training data based on correctness.
